newsitem.title: USA: Lake admits aides left him in dark on China probe.
newsitem.headline: Lake admits aides left him in dark on China probe.

text.p: President Bill Clinton's choice to head the troubled CIA acknowledged on Tuesday that his former National Security Council aides left him in the dark about an alleged Chinese plan to influence U.S. elections improperly.

At the start of twice-postponed, politically sensitive confirmation hearings, Anthony Lake said he had not been informed about the China matter by two of his staff who were briefed in June 1996 by the FBI.

"I should have been informed," Lake, Clinton's first-term national security adviser, said in reply to the first series of questions asked by Richard Shelby of Alabama, chairman of the Senate Select Committee on Intelligence.
Lake said National Security Adviser Sandy Berger, his then-deputy, also was left out of the loop on warnings about possible Chinese plans to hide illegal contributions to U.S. candidates.
But Lake, in reply to later questions, referred to the two former counterintelligence experts in question as "very fine career officers."

"I don't want to hang them out to dry," he said, adding he had deliberately avoided discussing the matter with them to avoid interfering with congressional and Justice Department investigations under way.

In his statement at the start of six scheduled days of hearings, Lake vowed if confirmed to head the sprawling, $30 billion-a-year U.S. espionage apparatus he would promote "from day one a climate of total accountability" for management failures.
"And if any officials fail to (keep their superiors fully informed), there must be a clear response: He or she will need to find another job," he said.

Lake dealt head-on with another potential problem raised by Republican critics -- whether he could give the president unbiased analyses if they indicted foreign policies he crafted as national security adviser.
"This is indeed an appropriate question. The answer, unequivocably, is 'yes'," Lake said. "I know firsthand how important it is to defend the bright line separating policy and intelligence."

In opening statements foreshadowing a bruising confirmation process, several Republicans cited concern about foreign policy issues over which Lake held sway, including the decision to keep Congress in the dark about Clinton's tacit approval of Iranian arms shipments to Bosnian Moslems in 1994.
"I have no apologies for the (Bosnia arms) policy," Lake said. "But I do appreciate that it would have been better to have informed key members of Congress on a discreet basis."

As director of central intelligence, Lake would head the Central Intelligence Agency and take overall responsibility for its 12 companion espionage outfits that together account for about $30 billion in annual outlays.

"I pledge to you that, if confirmed, I will not only fulfil every legal requirement in keeping Congress informed, but will go beyond," Lake said. He promised that when in doubt about sharing a secret with Congress, "my rule would be to inform" lawmakers.

Lake would be Clinton's third CIA director and the fifth person to hold the job in less than six years. He said the intelligence community has suffered from "turbulence and scandal," a possible reference to two convicted turncoats, an oft-changing leadership and disclosure of botched covert operations in Iraq and elsewhere.
Lake reiterated his previously stated intention to stay on as the nation's spy chief for four full years -- "the president, the Congress and fate willing."
